lesson.text: Quick memory: which three questions check a web page? (Who wrote it, when, and why?) Today: pictures and posts that can trick us.
Pictures can be edited: colours changed, things taken out or pasted in. Some pictures are made by computer programs and never happened at all.
Editing is not always bad: brightening a dark photo or making art is fine. A picture misleads when it tries to make you believe something that is not true.
Clues that a photo was changed: shadows pointing different ways, or light that doesn't match. Look for edges that are too sharp or too blurry round one thing, and patterns copied twice.
Worked example: in a sunny photo, the sun is on the left, so every shadow should fall to the right. The person's shadow falls to the left: they were pasted in from another photo.
A post can mislead with a real photo too: an old photo with a new, false caption, or a photo cut so you can't see what was around it.
Charts can mislead. This one starts at 50, not 0, so 52 and 55 look very different. Always read the numbers, not only the heights of the bars.
Try it in the world: with a grown-up, look at a surprising picture online. Can you find where it first came from, and when? Next: spreadsheets.

exercises.prompt: Every photo online shows exactly what happened.
exercises.hint: Think of photos that were edited or made by a computer.
exercises.explain: False: photos can be edited, or made by computer programs, or shown with false words.

exercises.prompt: The sun is on the left. One thing was pasted into this photo from another one. Which?
exercises.hint: Shadows fall away from the sun. Find the one that doesn't.
exercises.explain: The sun is on the left, so shadows fall to the right. The 2nd thing's shadow falls to the left: it was pasted in.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a clue that a photo was edited?
exercises.hint: Which one would be odd in a real sunny photo?
exercises.explain: In a real photo lit by the sun, every shadow points the same way. Shadows pointing different ways are a clue.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: editing that's fine, or editing that misleads?
items: a pasted-in shark called real news
an old photo posted as today's
exercises.hint: Is it trying to make people believe something false?
exercises.explain: Brightening a photo or a labelled joke is fine. A pasted-in shark called news and an old photo posted as today's mislead.

exercises.prompt: Moss's bar looks much taller. How many more gems did Moss really find than Pip?
exercises.hint: Read the numbers on the side, not the heights of the bars.
exercises.explain: Pip found 52 and Moss 55: 55 − 52 = 3 more. The axis starts at 50, which makes 3 look like a lot.

exercises.prompt: A post shows a real photo of snow with the words 'Snow in the desert today!', but it is an old mountain photo. What kind of trick is it?
exercises.hint: Is the photo itself changed, or only the words with it?
choices: a real photo with a false caption
a picture made by a computer
exercises.explain: The photo is real but the words are false: a real photo with a false caption.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for checking a surprising picture in order.
exercises.hint: The first step is to wait.
items: Look for clues like odd shadows
Check trusted news or ask a grown-up
Find where it first came from
Then decide whether to share it
exercises.explain: Stop, look for clues, find where it came from, check trusted news or a grown-up, then decide.

exercises.prompt: In a sunny photo, all the shadows fall away from the sun.
exercises.hint: Where is the light coming from?
exercises.explain: True: things block the sunlight, so their shadows fall on the side away from the sun.

exercises.prompt: The sun is on the right. One thing was pasted into this photo. Which?
exercises.hint: The sun is on the right, so which way should shadows fall?
exercises.explain: Shadows should fall to the left. The 3rd thing's shadow falls to the right, towards the sun: it was pasted in.

exercises.prompt: Why do some misleading charts start their axis above 0?
exercises.hint: What happens to the bars when the bottom of the chart is cut off?
choices: To make small differences look big
exercises.explain: Cutting off the bottom makes a small difference between bars look big.

exercises.prompt: Zara's bar looks 4 times as tall as Bram's. How many more gems did Zara really find?
exercises.hint: Read both numbers on the side, then take one from the other.
exercises.explain: Bram found 81 and Zara 84: 84 − 81 = 3 more. The axis starts at 80, so 3 looks 4 times as big.

exercises.prompt: Which headline is written to trick you into clicking?
exercises.hint: Which one hides the facts and shouts to make you curious?
choices: You won't BELIEVE what this cat did!!!
Cat finds its way home after 3 days
How to care for a new kitten
exercises.explain: It hides what happened and uses capitals and !!! to make you click. The others just say what they are about.

exercises.prompt: A picture made by a computer program can look like a real photo.
exercises.explain: True: some programs make pictures that look real but never happened, so check where a picture came from.

exercises.prompt: Someone sends you an odd picture of a friend that looks edited. What is best?
exercises.hint: How would your friend feel if it spread?
choices: Don't share it, and tell a trusted adult
exercises.explain: Don't share it: it could hurt your friend. Tell a trusted adult, who can help.

exercises.prompt: Match each trick to the clue that gives it away.
items: a cut axis on a chart
exercises.hint: Each trick leaves its own clue: in the light, the date, the numbers or the words.
exercises.explain: A pasted-in person's shadow falls the wrong way. An old photo can be traced to where it first appeared, years ago. A cut axis starts above 0, so small gaps look big. Clickbait hides the story behind capitals and !!!.
